mcqs.question: An app is off screen but the OS has frozen its process in memory, executing no code. Which state is it in?
options: Suspended
Background
Inactive
Not running
mcqs.explanation: Suspended means frozen in memory with no code executing — the OS can evict it at any moment with no further callback. Background still executes code on a time budget; inactive is a brief foreground state with events paused, not an off-screen state.

mcqs.question: Which delegate callback fires as the app transitions from Background toward Suspended?
options: applicationDidEnterBackground, followed shortly by suspension
None — the OS freezes the process without notifying it
applicationWillResignActive
applicationWillTerminate
mcqs.explanation: The Background-to-Suspended transition has no dedicated callback; the OS simply stops scheduling the process once it decides to freeze it. applicationDidEnterBackground already fired earlier, on the Inactive-to-Background transition.

mcqs.question: On an iPad running two windows of the same app, what is true about AppDelegate and SceneDelegate?
options: SceneDelegate replaced AppDelegate entirely as of iOS 13
Both windows share one SceneDelegate instance to coordinate state
There is one AppDelegate for the process and one SceneDelegate per open window
AppDelegate manages per-window UI state and SceneDelegate manages process launch
mcqs.explanation: AppDelegate is process-wide (one instance); each window gets its own SceneDelegate so two windows can independently background or foreground. AppDelegate still exists for process-level events like launch and push registration — it wasn't replaced.

mcqs.question: You start a short cleanup task in applicationDidEnterBackground using beginBackgroundTask, but never call endBackgroundTask on it. What happens?
options: Nothing — endBackgroundTask is optional if the task finishes on its own
The task automatically extends its own grace window indefinitely
iOS immediately suspends the app regardless of the task
The task looks like a hang to the OS, and future background scheduling for the app can be penalized
mcqs.explanation: Failing to call endBackgroundTask signals to iOS that the app isn't managing its background time responsibly, which can affect how much background time it's granted later. It doesn't extend the window or force immediate suspension on its own.

mcqs.question: A team saves critical user data only inside applicationWillTerminate. Why is this risky?
options: applicationWillTerminate runs on a background thread and can race with the save
applicationWillTerminate is deprecated and no longer called on modern iOS
A suspended app evicted for memory pressure, or a device reboot, never calls applicationWillTerminate at all
applicationWillTerminate only fires for apps using SceneDelegate, not AppDelegate
mcqs.explanation: The most common way apps die is silent eviction while suspended, which skips applicationWillTerminate entirely — it only fires for a running app being terminated in the foreground or a background task. The callback still exists and works; the risk is relying on it as the only save point.

mcqs.question: A large file upload kicked off in applicationDidEnterBackground with no expiration handling gets cut off mid-write in production, but never reproduces in the Xcode debugger. Why?
options: The debugger keeps the process alive past the normal background time budget
Debug builds are exempt from background execution limits
The upload actually completes instantly in debug builds due to a smaller binary
Xcode automatically wraps background tasks in a background task assertion
mcqs.explanation: A process attached to the debugger is generally not subject to the same background time limits, so the bug only shows up on a real device running untethered. Nothing about debug builds makes the upload itself faster or exempt from the OS's actual scheduling rules.
